Hellfire Chinese Language Pack Notes

Problem

After installing Hellfire, the interface is in English, and Chinese can’t be selected in the settings either. The Chinese language pack I previously installed for the AUR Firefox was useless — the reason is a version mismatch: Hellfire on Linux is 160.0, while that pack is for 157 and only recognizes 157.*. What’s more, it was installed in Firefox’s own profile, which Hellfire doesn’t read at all.

How it was solved on Linux

Hellfire’s profile is in ~/.mozilla/firefox/p9luzrhy.default-default. To determine which one to use specifically, look at LastVersion of compatibility.ini in each profile — the one whose version is 160.0 is the one.

  1. The official release 160.0 language pack hasn’t been published yet, so what was downloaded is the beta one: https://ftp.mozilla.org/pub/firefox/releases/160.0b2/linux-x86_64/xpi/zh-CN.xpi. In the pack, strict_max_version of manifest.json is 160.*, which covers exactly the needed version.
  2. Close the browser and copy it to <profile>/extensions/langpack-zh-CN@firefox.mozilla.org.xpi; the filename must be exactly the same, character for character.
  3. Add two lines in user.js:
  4. Restart. Once the language pack is recognized, the language list appears in the settings, and Chinese takes effect.

The second line only prevents manually placed packs from being automatically disabled; once it takes effect you can delete it, otherwise any extensions you manually put in later will all be automatically enabled.

What remains unclear: why at first no additional languages could be found in the settings. I checked Mozilla’s API, and it returns 103 languages for 160.0, so it’s not that the server has no packs. My guess is that the language list is cached, and only after a restart, when the cached locale became zh-CN, did it refresh and show up — but that’s just a guess.

The situation on Windows

Hellfire on Windows is 158.0.1, installed in C:\Tools\Firefox, with the profile in %APPDATA%\Mozilla\Hellfire\Profiles\64elc7uz.default-default-1. It already contains extensions\langpack-zh-CN@firefox.mozilla.org.xpi, which is the 158 language pack (strict_max_version is 158.*), and intl.locale.requested in prefs.js is also zh-CN,en-US. It’s the same approach as on Linux: a version-matching zh-CN pack placed in Hellfire’s own profile.

Note that the profile directory is Mozilla\Hellfire, not Mozilla\Firefox, and this machine doesn’t have a Mozilla\Firefox directory either. So the fact that “install Firefox and then uninstall it” used to work cannot simply be understood as the two browsers sharing the same profile. More likely, that step caused a version-matching 158 pack to land in Hellfire’s profile. Exactly how it landed there, I haven’t figured out.

If you run into the same thing on Windows in the future, there’s no need to install and uninstall Firefox again; just:

  1. Check the version with about:support.
  2. Download the pack for the corresponding version: https://ftp.mozilla.org/pub/firefox/releases/<版本>/win64/xpi/zh-CN.xpi; if the release version isn’t out yet, use the beta version number. The language pack itself is cross-platform; the contents under the win64 and linux-x86_64 directories are identical.
  3. about:addons → gear icon → Install Add-on From File, then select this .xpi.
  4. Select Chinese in about:preferences, then restart.

If “Install From File” is blocked, just copy it manually into the profile’s extensions\, the same as on Linux.

Things to remember

  • The language pack version must match the browser version. Once the browser’s major version updates, the old pack stops working and must be re-downloaded.
  • When the versions don’t match exactly, the interface will show partly Chinese and partly English. The incomplete translation with Mercury before was most likely due to this: strings newly added in the new version aren’t in the old pack.
  • If you use the beta pack, a few individual strings may differ slightly from the release version. Replace it once the release version comes out.

Notes on Installing Debian on ZTE F50 (MU300)

On 2026-10-26–27, I flashed a ZTE F50 storage version from B08 to B09, rooted it, shrank userdata, then installed Debian unstable (kernel 7.3), making it an Android + Debian dual-boot system. The first part covers daily usage; the latter part covers how it was installed, the pitfalls encountered, and reverse-engineering results.

1. Read This First: Daily Usage

Current State of the Device

ZTE F50 / MU300 storage version, Unisoc UMS9620, eMMC 234 GiB, no power button, no screen.

  • Android is B09 firmware (F50_FLYMODEM_ZYV1.0.0B09), rooted (Magisk 28.1, Shell authorized), installed in slot a, with userdata shrunk to about 30 GiB.
  • Linux is Debian forky/sid, kernel 7.3.0, installed in slot b and the 198 GiB area after userdata (ext4, about 191G usable). It boots Linux by default and falls back to Android only after 5 consecutive boot failures.
  • The bootloader shows locked; the patched trustos has been flashed, and Linux can still boot in the locked state.
  • Linux has only one user, wray (sudo, docker group, zsh + oh-my-zsh + powerlevel10k). The ubuntu user created by the installer has been deleted. root is locked (PermitRootLogin no); to get root, use sudo -i or adb shell.
  • Installed docker 28.5, ufw, neovim, fzf, zoxide, lsd, duf, fastfetch, git, curl, etc. Time zone Asia/Tokyo.
  • No SIM, so no cellular network. Internet access is via Wi-Fi (connected to the home router RayWrt, device IP 10.17.1.143), or using the computer as a proxy.
  • wray’s password is in F:\Projects\tmp\f50\wray-credentials.txt (plaintext; handle it yourself after use). The installation password in answers-install.txt has been erased.

Connecting to the Device

MethodCommandDescription
Wi-Fissh wray@10.17.1.143Use when the device is connected to the router; the IP is whatever the router assigns
USB networkssh wray@192.168.77.1USB cable directly connected to the computer, NCM NIC, driver-free on Windows 11; the computer gets 192.168.77.111
USB adbadb shellDirectly a root shell

SSH only accepts keys (the 3 keys in Windows’ ~/.ssh/authorized_keys: Wray-Arch ed25519, Wray-Win rsa, phone u0_a355). adb in Linux also only accepts keys from /etc/mu300/adb_keys (adb_auth=keys), and is not open to all computers. The ssh ubuntu@192.168.77.1 shown at the end of the installer is fixed text; actually use wray@.

When using adb in Git Bash with paths like /data/..., run export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 first; otherwise the path will be rewritten as a Windows path.

Switching Systems: A Pitfall You Must Remember

Running mu300-linux from Android to enter Linux is only a “one-time trial boot”; at this point /etc/mu300/default-boot is still android. Reboot directly in Linux with reboot and it returns to Android, which looks like “automatic fallback after reboot” but is actually by design. To make Linux the permanent default, run sudo mu300-next-boot linux once after entering it. This is now set (the content of default-boot is linux).

Instance on 2026-10-27: the boot log contains mu300-next-boot: default boot is not linux, nothing to do; the previous kernel log is in pstore and was a normal Restarting system, not a crash.

In Linux:

In Android (adb, root):

You must include MU300_BUSYBOX, because the busybox bundled with Magisk is broken on this device (--list is empty, readlink -f returns empty). Without it, it reports misc resolves outside /dev/block (), and status will also incorrectly determine that “boot_b is an Android image and Linux is not installed.” That is a misjudgment; Linux is not lost. Use the busybox from the installation package, and the filename must be exactly busybox (a multi-call binary looks up applets by argv[0]; changing the name causes applet not found):

After switching, status should show boot_b: the Linux boot image. When checking slot status, the output looks like slot a priority 15, tries 1, successful 1, slot b priority 14, tries 1, successful 0.

Fallback when there is no computer: cut power 5 times in a row during Linux boot, and it automatically returns to Android.

Wi-Fi: Connecting the Device to a Router

The SC2355 radio can only do one thing at a time: act as a hotspot (AP) or as a client (station). After connecting to a router, the device’s own hotspot FRayWrt turns off. Switching from hotspot to client requires a reboot; switching from client back to hotspot does not. Only WPA2 and WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode are supported; pure WPA3 and Wi-Fi 7 networks are rejected. USB’s 192.168.77.1 is unaffected.

If the radio is still in hotspot mode at this point, scan / connect will report “the radio is an access point right now … cannot turn it back into a client without a reboot”. This is not a fault; connect will save the network first and join after reboot. Enter the password interactively or with --password-file; do not put it on the command line (it will go into the journal and ps). The configuration is stored in /etc/mu300/wifi-client.conf (0600, root); its content is SSID, PSK, ENABLE=1, METRIC=50. After connecting, Wi-Fi uplink takes precedence over mobile data and can theoretically be shared to USB clients via NAT (not tested).

This device is already connected to the home router and joins automatically at boot (service mu300-wifi-client.service runs wifi-client up).

Giving the Device Temporary Internet Access (When There Is No Wi-Fi/SIM)

Right after installation the device had no Internet and the clock was wrong; the approach was to use the computer as a proxy:

If the clock is wrong, sync the time first (date -u -s @<时间戳>); otherwise TLS will fail. The device can now access the Internet directly via Wi-Fi, so this step is generally unnecessary.

Firewall

Inbound rules are now managed by ufw: deny inbound by default, allow outbound, deny forwarding, and only allow 22 (tcp/udp, including IPv6).

wifi-client ships with an nft table inet mu300_wifi_filter. Its original input chain dropped all inbound traffic on wlan0 except established connections, DHCP replies, and rate-limited ping, so the LAN could ping the device but could not SSH in (sshd itself listening on *:22 was fine). This input chain has now been removed, leaving only the forward chain (which prohibits forwarding to the intranet when sharing the uplink). wifi-client status should normally show shared with the LAN (internet only); if it shows mu300_wifi_filter is not as wifi-client puts it, the rules are inconsistent with what the script generates.

The patch script is F:\Projects\tmp\f50\tools\wifi-client.noinput.sh, and the original file is backed up as /opt/mu300/bin/wifi-client.orig2. The patch modifies an installed file; system upgrades or reinstalls will overwrite it, and it will need to be reapplied. The project’s own mu300_filter (/etc/mu300/firewall.nft) only handles the cellular interface, docker0, and br-*, and does not affect wlan0.

Daily Maintenance

adb in Linux and adb in Android are two separate things. The adbd on the Linux side is a static aarch64 program included in the image (/opt/mu300/bin/adbd), started at boot by mu300-adbd.service, which adds itself to the USB gadget (FunctionFS); it has nothing to do with the HTTP switch or Samba trigger in Android. Each time an adb connection ends, the gadget unbinds, and the script rebinds it, so it looks like a plug/unplug on the computer.

What to Do If Something Goes Wrong

Cannot connect via SSH. Ping first. If ping works but SSH does not, check sudo ufw status and wifi-client status. If ping does not work, first check whether the device has returned to Android (Android has no port 22).

Linux will not boot / want to see the previous log. The device retries by itself and returns to Android after 5 consecutive failures. In Android, you can mount the Linux root partition read-only to view the journal. The area offset was calculated during installation (38700843008); the root filesystem is in the ubuntu/ directory under the mount point:

The journal is in binary format; copy it to a computer (or WSL) and read it with journalctl --file=<文件>. The kernel log from the last crash is in Android’s /sys/fs/pstore/console-ramoops-0. Note that omitting MU300_OFF causes NO-EXT4 magic=0000, because the default offset is not this device’s area.

Android has no adb. After flashing B09 or a factory reset, adb is still available because persist.sys.usb.config=adb and persist.adb.tcp.port=5555 are stored in the persist partition. If it really is gone, see the later section “How Wireless adb Is Enabled” and use F:\Projects\tmp\f50\re\f50_wireless_adb.py.

Completely bricked. Short the test point to enter download mode and flash back using the original B08 backup.

Pitfalls to Avoid (Quick Reference)

  1. mu300-update has been renamed to .disabled. Its apply will replace the entire system with Ubuntu 24.04, destroying the self-built Debian. Do not repeatedly run this kind of updater; use apt to update Debian.
  2. The control panel and mu300-os treat this system as Ubuntu 26.04, with the version number displayed as empty; this is normal.
  3. Entering Linux from Android is only one-time; see above.
  4. Debian sid’s wpa_passphrase has a bug; the original wifi-client connect reports could not build the wpa_supplicant configuration, and it has been patched (full code later).
  5. The device has no python3 or openssl; write scripts with sh / awk / sed.
  6. sid is a rolling release; think before full-upgrade, because if something goes wrong there is no official image to roll back to.
  7. The hotspot country code COUNTRY=TR is the project default; in Japan it should be changed to JP and has not been changed yet.
  8. Repeatedly running the “temporary wireless adb tool” is destructive; do not do that (see below).

2. Where the Files Are

ContentPath
Original B08 backup (73 partitions, including calinv / nr_fixnv / prodnv / persist / ztepersist / ztecfg)O:\F50\F50_储存版B08_一键Root+永久禁用系统更新\backup_3146\

The zte-f50-toolkit git repository only has the macOS version; the full Windows version is in the zip of release releasev1.

Also, large files on the computer that can be deleted are F:\Projects\tmp\f50\debian\release\ (487 MiB original release asset) and F:\Projects\tmp\f50\toolkit-win\f50-downgrade-unlock-modempatch.zip (1 GB). Files containing plaintext passwords are wray-credentials.txt and answers-install.txt. In WSL, /home/wray/work/debian-sid and image mu300-debian:sid have been deleted, while the arm64 binfmt registration is kept; there is also about 11 GB of docker build cache that can be cleaned with docker builder prune -f, which has not been done yet. The temporary apt/docker proxy configuration on the device was deleted after environment setup was completed.

3. How It Was Installed

1. Entering Download Mode (The Biggest Pitfall on This Device)

Directly connecting --kickto 2 always fails on this device: the log shows kick reboot timeout, but spd_dump’s exit code is 0, and there is also pause at the end of the bat file. It looks like a normal finish, but not a single byte was actually written. The earlier “flashed B09 but it is still B08” was very likely this.

What works is the “short-circuit mode” command, without --kickto, manually loading FDL1 and FDL2:

The procedure is: unplug the cable → short the test point → keep it shorted and plug in the cable (it does not matter whether the command is started first or is already connected). A single occurrence of usb_send failed (0 / 1) means unstable contact; start over. Whether it succeeds depends only on Write Part Done in the log, not on the exit code.

2. Flashing B09 (Erasing userdata)

Before any flashing, first confirm you have the original B08 backup; flashing the ROM will overwrite device partitions such as ztepersist and splloader.

It writes all .bin under zte-f50-b09\ (including splloader, ztepersist, the 2GB super, misc), about 2.7GB in total.

3. root + Patched trustos

It only writes trustos_a and boot_a for the current slot (slot a) and does not erase userdata. f50b09_t.bin is 5178856 bytes (MD5 prefix a110ecb1), the same as trustos.bin in the author’s package. The boot used is magiskf50b09.img (0e9e8a4d); the author kkroot’s boot.bin (f2e8db4a) is another file; both are Magisk images. After flashing, ro.boot.flash.locked still shows 1, but Linux can boot.

4. adb

After flashing B09 or a factory reset following userdata shrinking, adb is still available: this ROM includes UFI-TOOLS (com.minikano.f50_sms) and the Magisk stub; persist.sys.usb.config=adb and persist.adb.tcp.port=5555 are stored in the persist partition and survive a factory reset. Only the first time right after flashing B09 do you need to enable it with the “temporary wireless adb tool” (see Part 5). The firmware’s adbd does not verify keys: ro.adb.secure=1, but it can connect even if /data/misc/adb/adb_keys does not exist, and pairing is not required.

5. Magisk

  1. adb install Magisk_28103_origin.apk. After rooting, only the stub is on the device, and the version shows 1.0.
  2. Open the app and do “repair environment”, then reboot.
  3. Connect to the screen with scrcpy and grant root permission to Shell.
  4. adb shell su -c id should be uid=0. Before repair, su is not in PATH; only /debug_ramdisk/su exists.

After the factory reset triggered by shrinking userdata, the Magisk app is still there, but you need to repair once more and authorize once more.

6. Installer and Shrinking userdata

The installer uses the PowerShell version install.ps1 (this machine has no lz4). Before running it in Git Bash, three environment pitfalls must be handled first:

Read-only check: install.ps1 -Check -Lang en.

Shrinking userdata uses an answer file (-AnswersFile). For answer variables, see the header comments of install.sh. If any variable is missing, the installer reports no answer to the question ... set MU300_ANS_xxx at the prompt and aborts, and when it aborts nothing has been written.

Result: userdata shrank from 228.19 GiB to 30.19 GiB, leaving 198.00 GiB free after it, and Android went through recovery to factory reset.

7. Installing the Debian Package

Continuing the installation with a custom package fails: The prepared installation cannot be continued: this installer's tools or the package differ. The reason is that the payload identity in the transaction was calculated during shrinking (when there was no package), and the identity changes when installing the custom package. The workaround is to add -NoResume. At the start of the area there is a token written by the installer itself; it will prompt “unpartitioned space is not empty”, so answer MU300_ANS_OVERWRITE=overwrite (this area was carved out by yourself, and you confirm it is empty).

Complete answer file:

Command:

After installation the device automatically reboots into Linux. In this installation log, the area offset is 38700843008, size 198.0 GiB, ext4 is created, and it writes the Linux area, boot_b, and a 32-byte misc, without touching boot_a, GPT, or userdata.

After installation, /etc/mu300/adb on the device is on and adb_auth is keys, meaning USB adb only allows keys from /etc/mu300/adb_keys.

8. Post-Installation Environment Setup

When the device was set up it had no Internet and the clock was stuck at Oct 17. So the flow was: run tools/proxy.py on the computer (a minimal HTTP/CONNECT proxy listening only on 127.0.0.1:7890) → adb reverse tcp:7890 tcp:7890 → sync the time in the device first → temporarily write the apt proxy /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99tmp-proxy and the docker drop-in 99tmp-proxy.conf → run tools/setup-env.sh as root on the device. device-online.sh on|off wraps these steps as a switch, and off deletes the proxy configuration on the device and stops the proxy.

The script installed: zsh git sudo curl ca-certificates zoxide fzf lsd duf neovim fastfetch openssh-server docker.io docker-cli docker-compose. User wray was created with useradd -m -s /usr/bin/zsh -G sudo,docker, and the SSH public keys were taken from Windows’ authorized_keys (3 keys). Note that the script is sent to the device via heredoc; unescaped $(...) inside it will be expanded early on the computer, so the password must be set separately with chpasswd. oh-my-zsh + powerlevel10k + zsh-autosuggestions + zsh-syntax-highlighting were all installed; .zshrc and .p10k.zsh were taken from wray-lee/dotfiles (the archlinux plugin in zshrc is harmless on Debian; the clash/nas/n2n aliases are from the original machine’s configuration and do not work here). Docker 28.5.2 uses overlay2, cgroup v2 + systemd; /etc/docker/daemon.json limits the log size, and docker run hello-world passes (pulling images through the proxy).

Verified after reboot: 192.168.77.1 is reachable after about 1 minute; SSH (key-based), docker, kernel 7.3.0, and mu300-update disabled all persist. The first systemctl is-system-running was degraded (leaving a failed marker), and it recovered after systemctl reset-failed.

9. Current USB Network State

The USB gadget is NCM (Windows 11 has built-in driver UsbNcm Host Device, so no driver installation is needed). usb0 and wlan0 are bridged into br-lan; the device IP is 192.168.77.1/24, the device side provides DHCP and DNS, and the computer gets 192.168.77.111 (NIC name “Ethernet 8”), restoring automatically after reboot. Kernel ip_forward=1. The NAT (masquerade) to the uplink is added by mu300-mobile-data.service after mobile data connects, and this device has no SIM (+CME ERROR: 10, log no card in SIM1), so the computer cannot access the Internet via USB for now. After inserting a SIM, in theory 5G would automatically be shared with the computer via USB and Wi-Fi hotspot FRayWrt (SSID and password already imported from Android), but this has not been tested. Conversely, “computer gives the device Internet access” requires no configuration change; use device-online.sh above. If you want to make it Windows ICS, administrator privileges are required; this was not done.

4. How This Debian Image Was Made

This is not the project’s official image. The official project only releases Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 and OpenWrt; the Debian 13 build in docs/DISTROS.md only says “same package names as Ubuntu” and has not been tested on real hardware. This image was built by a background agent in WSL.

  • The base is debian:unstable (arm64, requires qemu binfmt). Dockerfile patches: docker-compose-v2 changed to docker-compose, and docker-cli added.
  • Patches to assemble.sh: KREL and UBUNTU can be overridden with MU300_KREL and MU300_UBUNTU_RELEASE; added /release mount to reuse the release’s bundled opt/mu300, etc/mu300, etc.; fixed the issue where an NTFS checkout caused the overlay to become 1000:1000 / 0777 (even /, /etc, and /usr were set to 777), restoring ownership and permissions according to the release manifest.
  • Kept the identities and filenames of SYSTEM=ubuntu-26.04 and OS=ubuntu in the manifest to pass the installer’s whitelist, replaced only the rootfs payload, updated SHA256_ROOTFS and SHA256SUMS, and removed the signature (the package is unsigned and only for local use).
  • Reused the release’s static aarch64 helper programs (logdw, adbd, mu300-keys, mu300-bt-init, mu300-carry); kernel modules come from mu300-kernel-7.3.tar.gz (3059 .ko), and the kernel was not compiled from source.
  • Artifacts: rootfs mu300-ubuntu-26.04-rootfs.tar.gz (261.7 MiB, 834 MiB unpacked, SHA256 5e5797470b61810c32d2d51b111ba6f9667b91aea0e0e7e373b39896ccb48bf2), whole package 319.8 MiB.
  • Verification: the installer’s package_load / package_verify output PACKAGE OK; dpkg --audit is clean; apt was tested successfully against deb.debian.org; key components are all present.

Known risks:

  • mu300-update apply will replace the entire system with Ubuntu 24.04 (Debian does not have VERSION_ID, so it falls back to the Ubuntu rootfs). Handled: /opt/mu300/bin/mu300-update and /usr/local/bin/mu300-update were renamed to .disabled, and mu300-update-notice.timer has been disabled. The control panel’s update interface returns unsupported when the binary is missing; mu300-accounts.service only calls it when a marker file exists (normally it does not).
  • The panel and mu300-os treat it as Ubuntu 26.04, with the version number displayed as empty.
  • sid is a rolling release, so build results drift with the date.
  • No SIM, so modem and mobile data were not tested; Wi-Fi hotspot, Bluetooth, and GPU were also not verified item by item.

5. The sid Bug in the Wi-Fi Client and the Patch

When connecting to the router, wifi-client connect reports could not build the wpa_supplicant configuration.

Troubleshooting process. The user first saw “the radio is an access point right now … cannot scan either” (a normal prompt); after following the prompt and running connect, the above error appeared. grep -n "could not build the wpa_supplicant" /opt/mu300/bin/wifi-client located it at line 832, which calls network_block() (around lines 733–755). In the function, h=$(printf '%s\n' "$2" | wpa_passphrase "$1" | sed … psk=<64位hex>); if h is empty, it does return 1. Trying printf '%s\n' testpass1234 | wpa_passphrase test directly on the device produced no output at all.

Root cause. In Debian sid’s wpasupplicant 2.11, when wpa_passphrase reads the password from a pipe, it calls tcgetattr on stdin, which fails on a non-terminal with no output, so network_block() cannot get the PSK hash. The older Ubuntu version does not have this problem.

Patch approach. If wpa_passphrase succeeds, use the hash as before; if it fails, fall back to psk="密码" and let wpa_supplicant calculate PBKDF2 itself. The password length must be 8–63 characters. The configuration file is 0600 root; the SAE path already writes plaintext sae_password, so the security is equivalent. Unit-verified outputs for WPA2, WPA2/WPA3 (SAE), open network, and short password (returns failure) are all correct. Limitation: there may be problems when the password contains non-ASCII characters or double quotes; this was not tested.

Complete fixed version of network_block() (replacing the function of the same name in /opt/mu300/bin/wifi-client, around lines 733–760; everything else unchanged):

The only difference from the original is this one place:

Apply: On the device, as root:

Rollback: cp -p /opt/mu300/bin/wifi-client.orig /opt/mu300/bin/wifi-client.

The patch script replaces by line number (lines 742–743) using awk; in the generated file, \t and \n become literal tabs and newlines (inside single quotes the output is equivalent and syntactically correct, just not pretty); the version above is a manually cleaned-up version with equivalent content. If a future project upgrade changes the line numbers, the patch script will modify the wrong lines, so manual patching should be used instead.

Verification function (does not touch the network):

Fix for LAN SSH being blocked (another place in the same script). rules_text generates an nft transaction, and fw_state compares the current ruleset against it line by line; if anything extra is found, it is judged as unknown, so fail_closed. Therefore you cannot simply add another accept to the input chain. This time the approach was to remove the input chain entirely, so that rules_text only generates the forward chain; generation and comparison use the same function, so both sides match, and wifi-client status remains shared with the LAN (internet only). Specifically, the change is in rules_text, in the few lines printf from chain input to the input chain counter drop, with the beginning changed to directly table inet %s { chain forward {. After the change, wifi-client reconnect takes effect. Verification: computer (10.17.1.x) ssh wray@10.17.1.143 passes. Side effect: the device has no inbound filtering at all on Wi-Fi, so it must rely on ufw.

6. Reverse-Engineering Results for the “Temporary Wireless ADB Tool” and the Wireless adb Mechanism

1. Sample

Analyzed was opener.exe (the original is O:\F50\临时打开无线ADB工具【…】.exe), completed by the background agent using static unpacking + Unicorn emulation + Go disassembly.

  • SHA256 34a7ebf72fb636e34cbffa4981f2a7bffbb88c9e51a463b67ec759977432edf6.
  • PE32+ x86-64, Go 1.23.7, custom NM$L packer, Garble obfuscation (function names changed, strings decrypted at runtime).
  • The payload in the packer is compressed with LZMA raw (lc=7, lp=0, pb=4); after decompression it is 38,743,273 bytes, VA = file offset + 0x140001000.
  • Four files are embedded: AdbWinUsbApi.dll, AdbWinApi.dll, adb.exe, zreq.exe. zreq.exe is a 32-bit Go program (source path /Users/kano/GolandProjects/awesomeProject/main.go), with SHA256 matching O:\F50\kkfile\bin\zreq.exe. This version does not have adb.com / zreq.com; those may be from another version.

First, a correction to my earlier wrong judgment: I once said it sends AT commands in 6 steps over serial port \\.\COM%u; that was wrong. The sample contains no serial APIs at all (no SetCommState, GetCommState, SetupComm, PurgeComm, COMMTIMEOUTS, DCB, and no COM1..9 or 115200), and the \\.\COM%u string in memory comes from a Go standard library path constant. The message “Cannot operate the port, please rerun this program” is not a serial error either: it is printed in step 1 when the literal result cannot be found in zreq‘s stdout, and “port” refers to the USB port mode USB_PORT_SETTING. In the real trace, zreq … usb_port_switch=0 hung for about 25 seconds and then exactly this sentence appeared. Lesson: strings in memory dumps are obfuscated; use real static unpacking.

2. The Six Steps

StepChannelTargetContent
1/6HTTP goform (zreq)192.168.0.1:8080USB_PORT_SETTING&usb_port_switch=0 (turn off first); if stdout does not contain result, report “cannot operate port” and exit
2/6HTTP goformSame as aboveUSB_PORT_SETTING&usb_port_switch=1 (turn on again)
3/6HTTP goformSame as aboveREBOOT_DEVICE (reboot device)
4/6adb USBDeviceadb wait-for-device; on success print “found device.”
5/6adb shell USBDeviceThe 10 commands below; cat smb.conf output must contain adbd, otherwise “configuration failed!”
6/6SMB (TCP 445)192.168.0.1Guest (capital G) / empty password; list shares, skip IPC$ / ADMIN$ / C$, mount normal shares and ReadDir("."), total timeout 100 seconds; on failure report “verification failed!”
Afterwardadb TCP192.168.0.1:5555adb connect 192.168.0.1

The 10 commands in step 5 (verbatim):

The original program’s idea was: the “switch” for wireless adb is Samba’s preexec = start adbd; each time someone (Guest) connects to an SMB share, Samba executes start adbd, and adbd reads service.adb.tcp.port / persist.adb.tcp.port = 5555 and starts listening. But in actual testing this was not the key on this firmware (see below).

3. HTTP Login Algorithm (zreq)

Base address http://192.168.0.1:8080; request headers User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0, Referer: http://<ip>:8080/index.html, Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, Cookie: <登录后 Set-Cookie 的第一段>.

  • LD: GET /goform/goform_get_cmd_process?isTest=false&cmd=LD&_=<毫秒> → LD in JSON.
  • Login: H1 = SHA256(password).upper(), H2 = SHA256(H1 + LD).upper(), POST /goform/goform_set_cmd_process, body goformId=LOGIN&isTest=false&password=<H2>, take the first segment of Set-Cookie as the Cookie. The default password is in the script (f50_wireless_adb.py‘s DEFAULT_PWD).
  • Get version information: GET …cmd=Language,cr_version,wa_inner_version&multi_data=1; get RD: GET …cmd=RD.
  • AD: H3 = SHA256(wa_inner_version + cr_version).upper(), AD = SHA256(H3 + RD).upper() (note it is RD, not the JSESSIONID used in the U20 script).
  • The final POST body is generated by Go’s url.Values.Encode(), i.e. sorted by key.

4. What USB_PORT_SETTING Actually Does in the Web Backend

From decompiling /system/priv-app/ZteWebServer/ZteWebServer.apk (process com.zte.web, listening on 8080, sharedUserId=android.uid.system). The full report is in F:\Projects\tmp\f50\zteweb\notes\.

USB_PORT_SETTING does only one thing: write the system setting Settings.Global adb_enabled (1 is on, 0 is off, any other value is treated as 0). It does not write persist.sys.usb.config / sys.usb.config, does not call UsbManager, does not execute shell, does not send broadcasts, does not reboot, and returns success even if it does not actually take effect. The status query cmd=usb_port_switch also reads adb_enabled, not the real USB state.

What actually takes effect is system_server (evidence from services.jar in the B09 backup of the same device):

  • AdbService.setAdbEnabled() continues only when the value actually changes; if it is the same value, it returns directly. On a real change, it does ctl.start adbd / ctl.stop adbd and calls back UsbDeviceManager.
  • UsbDeviceManager.setAdbEnabled(): on → persist.sys.usb.config="adb"; off → "charging"; then reconfigure sys.usb.config.
  • At boot, AdbService.systemReady() does the reverse: reads persist.sys.usb.config; if it contains adb, set adb_enabled to 1, otherwise 0, overwriting the value last written into Settings by the web page.
  • In init: on post-boot && property:sys.usb.config=none → setprop sys.usb.config ${persist.sys.usb.config}; on property:sys.usb.config=adb && property:sys.usb.configfs=1 → start adbd.
  • SettingsProvider also does not notify observers when “writing the same value”, so repeatedly writing 1 is a complete no-op.

REBOOT_DEVICE first returns success, then after 500ms PowerManager.reboot("manualreboot"). UsbTools (write rndis,diag,diag_mdm,adb when on, write rndis when off, and finally reboot unconditionally) is only called by DEVELOPER_MODE_SETTING / SET_DEVICE_MODE, while this APK’s DeveloperModule only registers USB_PORT_SETTING, so this path is unreachable on this firmware. The web UI is index.html#usb_port → js/adm/usb_port.js; what is submitted is goformId=USB_PORT_SETTING + usb_port_switch=1/0, and you must click Apply for the request to be sent; just clicking the radio does not send it. The APK contains no code that writes service.adb.tcp.port / persist.adb.tcp.port or starts/stops adbd; the persist.adb.tcp.port=5555 on the device is a persistent property that the ROM already has.

5. “How to Enable It When There Is No adb”

  • Wired adb: make adb_enabled undergo a real 0→1 change. The framework will immediately ctl.start adbd, write persist.sys.usb.config as adb, and reconfigure USB; code-wise, no reboot is needed. REBOOT_DEVICE just makes the USB reassemble stably after reboot according to persist=adb, and is the most reliable approach.
  • Why only clicking the switch on the web page does not work: if the switch was already 1 (what the UI shows is adb_enabled, which is neither persist nor the actual adbd state), submitting 1 again is the same value and is short-circuited by two layers into a no-op; persist.sys.usb.config is not written as adb, and at reboot systemReady() recalculates from persist and goes back to 0, so there is still no adb, while the UI keeps showing ON. The original tool first sends 0 and then 1, which forces a real 1→0→1 change. To do it manually: on the web page, turn it off first, click Apply, then turn it on, and click Apply again.
  • Secondary possibilities: the radio was clicked but Apply was not; the reboot happened before the asynchronous persist write; under certain SIM states, ZTE_ADB_USB_SECURITY_RESTRICTION forcibly turns off adb; adbd or the USB endpoint is stuck and requires re-enumeration.
  • TCP listening for wireless adb: at startup, adbd reads service.adb.tcp.port / persist.adb.tcp.port; this ROM includes persist.adb.tcp.port=5555, so adbd listens on TCP 5555 as soon as it starts. The Samba approach can neither be done on this firmware (smb.conf is immutable) nor is it necessary.

On-site confirmation (when the device is in Android, query after logging in to the web interface): usb_port_switch → '1', developer_mode_enable → '1'; on the device settings get global adb_enabled = 1, persist.sys.usb.config = adb, sys.usb.config = rndis,mtp,adb, init.svc.adbd = running, persist.adb.tcp.port = 5555. The two diagnostic interfaces can be used after login without adb:

  • GET /goform/goform_get_cmd_process?isTest=false&cmd=usb_port_switch → adb_enabled
  • GET /goform/goform_get_cmd_process?isTest=false&cmd=developer_mode_enable → whether persist.sys.usb.config contains adb

If the former is 1 and the latter is 0, that is the branch described above where “the UI shows ON but persist has no adb”; just do 0 then 1.

Risk: sending usb_port_switch=0 alone (a real 1→0) will write persist.sys.usb.config as charging; if the subsequent 1 does not succeed, after reboot USB will only have charging, and RNDIS / ECM and the web backend may both become unreachable. Do not send 0 alone when you have no recovery method; if the original program or our script fails after step 1, this is the bad state left behind. The framework-side evidence comes from the B09 backup image of the same device; if the device is not running this firmware, the details of services.jar may differ.

6. Alternative Script and Real-Device Testing (2026-10-27)

Script F:\Projects\tmp\f50\re\f50_wireless_adb.py (standard library only; the SMB trigger is optional and uses impacket, installed at F:\Projects\tmp\f50\tools\venv). By default it only prints the plan; you must add --yes to execute. With --yes, it reboots like the original tool; if you do not want a reboot, add --no-reboot. --login-only --yes only logs in and calculates AD, without modifying the device.

Test environment: device in Android (B09, Magisk root); the computer’s Wi-Fi connects to the device’s own hotspot FRayWrt (computer 192.168.0.50, device 192.168.0.1). The starting point was a stuck USB adb transport (adb devices could not see the device, while ADB Interface was still present in Device Manager), exactly the “recover via HTTP when there is no adb” scenario.

StageResult
Read-only --login-only --yesPassed: login and AD were both calculated; the reverse-engineered login algorithm matches the real device
USB_PORT_SETTING=0Passed
USB_PORT_SETTING=1Failed the first time (a bug in the script itself; see below), passed after fixing
REBOOT_DEVICE + adb wait-for-devicePassed: USB adb came back by itself after reboot
sed -i changed to smb.confFailed: Operation not permitted; smb.conf has the immutable attribute (lsattr is ----i----E), and the original program cannot do it on this firmware either
SMB Guest triggerNo valid result (step 5 was not written)
adb connect 192.168.0.1:5555Failed: 10053 / 10060; on the device, [::]:5555 is listening and iptables filter INPUT defaults to ACCEPT, but the computer cannot get in over Wi-Fi; the cause was not determined

Things fixed in the script:

  1. Cookie reuse caused the second login to fail: after logging in at step 1, the old Cookie was carried into step 2’s login request; the device returned {"result":0} and did not send Set-Cookie, reporting login: no Set-Cookie. The original program used a new zreq process for each step, with no Cookie at login. Changed so that each login() clears the Cookie first. This problem can leave the device in a state with USB debugging off, and is also the source of similar side effects in the original program.
  2. Default behavior changed back to match the original program (--yes causes a reboot; previously the default skipped the reboot, which prevented USB adb from coming up).
  3. Added a pure-Python SMB trigger implementation impacket (Windows rejects Guest SMB by default, and there is no smbclient).
  4. Steps 5 and 6 changed to best-effort: on failure only warn, continue trying adb connect, and judge by whether adb ultimately connects.

Other findings:

  • Wired adb only needs the HTTP USB_PORT_SETTING plus a reboot.
  • After reboot, sys.usb.config changed from rndis,mtp,adb to ecm,mtp,adb. Windows has no ECM NIC driver, so the computer’s USB NIC disappears, and the HTTP channel is only reliable over Wi-Fi (connecting to the device hotspot).
  • The device’s iptables INPUT only allows 8080 from source 192.168.0.0/24; 8080 coming in from adb forward‘s loopback is dropped.
  • persist.sys.usb.config was adb both before and after the experiment; setprop persist.sys.usb.config adb,rndis in the script did not take effect under the shell identity.
  • When both USB adb and 192.168.0.1:5555 devices are present, the command reports more than one device; first adb disconnect.
  • The original program sends usb_port_switch=0 first each time and does not recover on failure; running it repeatedly changes persist.sys.usb.config from adb,rndis to adb and makes 192.168.0.1 temporarily unreachable, so do not run it repeatedly.

Restoration after testing: the 12 temporary files left by the sed failure in /data/samba/etc/ (smb.conf plus 6 random characters) and the smb.conf.bak.opener created by the script were all deleted; the MD5 of smb.conf is the same before and after (cf419aec312cf4b6abaa849d67e31093), and the immutable attribute was not touched. The USB debugging switch ended up on, and persist.adb.tcp.port=5555 and persist.sys.usb.config=adb are the same as before testing. A harmless /data/local/tmp/bbdir/busybox remains on the Android side (it is needed to switch to Linux; do not delete it).

The pitfall encountered when switching back to Linux was the Magisk busybox issue mentioned earlier. Also observed: the MD5 of boot_b produced by dd (9d7a4a10…) does not match the work/boot-linux-slotb.img pushed during installation (029289…), but the content is a Linux image (contains the mu300 string, no Magisk, boots normally); the cause was not investigated (possibly the installer processed it before writing, or it was updated after first boot).

7. Unfinished and Unverified

  • Verify mobile data and USB Internet sharing after inserting a SIM.
  • Verify item by item the Wi-Fi hotspot (reboot back to AP mode), Bluetooth, GPU, and modem.
  • Why the computer times out accessing 192.168.0.1:5555 over Wi-Fi was not determined (need to check ip6tables, raw / mangle tables, hostapd client isolation, and whether adbd only listens on loopback).
  • Confirm whether enabling adb for the first time on a brand-new device likewise only requires the HTTP 0→1 plus a reboot.
  • Change the hotspot country code COUNTRY=TR to JP.
  • To automatically grant Shell Magisk root permission from Android, you could investigate presetting policies with magisk --sqlite after root; not tried.
  • Automation ideas: backup verification, B09 writing, trustos + boot writing (device already in download mode), Magisk installation, --check, answer-file-driven shrinking and installation, and post-install environment setup (setup-env.sh) can all be scripted; what must be done manually is shorting the test point, granting Shell authorization after Magisk repair, and enabling adb for the first time on a brand-new device.

Goal: All container traffic accessing the public internet goes through the WARP exit; the host’s own traffic, externally mapped ports, and intranet access such as ZeroTier / NetBird remain unchanged.

Example: 192.236.240.51 (Ubuntu 22.04, script at /root/warp/)

1. Approach

Do not modify the host’s default route. Use only policy routing to steer traffic whose source address belongs to the Docker subnet (172.16.0.0/12) into a separate routing table (table 200). The default route in this table is the WireGuard interface warp.

Several types of traffic need to be excluded (all returned to the main table):

RuleEffectConsequence of omitting
101 fwmark 0x40000/0x40000 lookup mainFor connections entering from eth0 (mapped ports such as -p 7080:7080), reply packets go out via eth0Reply packets are sent into WARP; all external access to mapped ports times out
102 from 172.16/12 to 10.0.0.0/8 lookup mainContainer access to ZeroTier / NetBird and other overlay intranetsContainer access to internal addresses such as 10.17.1.200 fails
102 from 172.16/12 to 192.168.0.0/16 lookup mainOther private networksSame as above
103 from 172.16/12 to 172.16/12 lookup mainContainer-to-container traffic and container access to the host bridgeInter-container communication breaks
104 from 172.16/12 lookup 200All remaining traffic goes through WARP—

The marking for 101 is applied via conntrack:

The marking bit uses 0x40000 to avoid conflict with NetBird’s 0x1bd00 (rule 110).

Also required:

2. Obtain WARP configuration (wgcf)

/root/warp/warp.conf retains only fields recognized by wg setconf (must not contain Address/DNS/MTU):

Endpoint pitfalls (tested on this machine):

  • engage.cloudflareclient.com:2408 / [2606:4700:d0::a29f:c001]:2408 consistently fail to handshake on this machine.
  • After the interface is newly created, the first endpoint’s handshake often gets no reply (tcpdump only shows outbound 148-byte packets); switching to another port enables handshake immediately and it remains stable thereafter. Therefore, you cannot rely on hard-coding a single endpoint; automatic rotation is required.
  • Available ports (Cloudflare WARP official port pool): 854 859 864 878 880 890 891 894 903 908 928 934 939 942 943 945 946 955 968 987 988 1002 1010 1014 1018 1070 1074 1180 1387 1701 1843 2371 2408 2506 3138 3476 3581 3854 4177 4198 4233 4500 5279 5956 7103 7152 7156 7281 7559 8319 8742 8854 8886

3. Script /root/warp/setup.sh

Key design points:

  • Rule 104 is added only after a successful handshake. The previous version added 104 from startup; once WARP handshake failed, all containers (openclaw’s Telegram/Slack, etc.) lost network connectivity.
  • fail-open: When WARP is unavailable, containers fall back to using the host IP directly. The cost is that during this period the exit IP is exposed as the VPS IP. If a service must use the WARP IP, change route_off so it does not delete 104 (fail-closed).
  • Handshake freshness threshold is 180 seconds (with WireGuard traffic or keepalive, re-handshake occurs every 120 seconds).

4. systemd

Prevent rules from being cleared by systemd-networkd: networkd by default deletes policy routing rules that were “not created by it” (this is likely why rule 104 mysteriously disappeared previously). Added:

(Takes effect only when networkd restarts; even if the rules are deleted, the check timer will restore 104 within 1 minute. If 101-103 are lost, re-run systemctl restart warp-egress.)

5. Verification

6. Notes

  • Host processes do not go through WARP (running curl directly on the host exits via the VPS IP). When needed, use --interface warp.
  • Newly created containers have an MTU of 1500; setup.sh up only changes containers that are running at that moment to 1380. TCP has MSS clamping as a fallback, but large UDP packets may be fragmented. When needed, use systemctl restart warp-egress.
  • Container access to host bridge addresses such as 172.17.0.1:<端口> goes through rule 103 and is unrelated to WARP. If a service only binds to 127.0.0.1, containers originally cannot access it; use the service name within the same Docker network instead.
  • ZeroTier has already added the warp interface to interfacePrefixBlacklist in local.conf to avoid ZT attempting to punch holes through WARP.

OpenWrt DS-Lite (IPv4 over IPv6)

Why Japanese broadband commonly uses DS-Lite

The traditional method (PPPoE) queues at NTT’s network termination equipment (BRAS, responsible for PPPoE authentication and assigning IPv4),
and speeds drop severely during evening peak hours. The reason is that NTT’s BRAS expansion standard is calculated by number of connected users (sessions),
not by actual traffic: per-user traffic has increased more than tenfold, but if the session count has not reached the threshold, capacity is not expanded.
Who bears the expansion cost (NTT or the ISP) has also remained disputed, so this problem has dragged on for many years without being solved.

The workaround is to have ISPs build their own IPv6 networks (IPoE / v6plus, Xpass),
so traffic does not pass through the BRAS. But pure IPv6 cannot access IPv4 websites, so IPv4 packets are encapsulated in an IPv6 tunnel,
and decapsulated by the gateway on the ISP side (AFTR)—this is DS-Lite (RFC 6333).
Another similar scheme in Japan is MAP-E (JPNE/KDDI-affiliated), while DS-Lite is used by NTT-affiliated ISPs.

Cost: behind the AFTR is carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT), and home routers cannot get a public IPv4 address,
so port forwarding/self-hosted services require another approach (use IPv6 or NAT traversal).

OpenWrt Configuration

1. Install packages

After installation, restart LuCI or the router.

2. Create an interface

Network → Interfaces → Add new interface:

  • Name: dslite (fill in this name in the later traffic-splitting script)
  • Protocol: Dual-Stack Lite (RFC6333)
  • AFTR address: prefer an IPv6 address; do not enter a domain name

When entering a domain name (e.g. dgw.xpass.jp), the router must first resolve the AAAA record before it can establish the tunnel,
and this process depends on wan6’s DNS—if the connection has just been dialed and DNS is not ready yet, resolution fails,
so the DS-Lite interface remains unable to connect. Entering an IP directly skips this step.

ISPAFTR domainAFTR IPv6 address
Rakuten Hikari (Xpass)dgw.xpass.jp2001:f60:0:200::1:1

GT7 (RMX6688) Port Package AOD Fix / Backup Work Log

Device: realme GT7 China hardware RMX6688 (project number 24618), serial number 3B1F5TE6K0YF1PRM, rooted (KernelSU).
Flashed with a port package: International version RMX5061 EX01 → China hardware.

Iron rule: Not a bit of data may be lost. Only read-only operations are performed on the phone. fastboot flash/erase/format/-w/set_active, setprop/resetprop persist, rm or writes to /data, and factory reset must each first obtain the user’s explicit consent. Before flashing, the backup must first pass verification and have already been copied to a second disk.

1. Current version composition of the phone (verified 2026-10-11)

LayerVersion
Upper layer (system / product, etc.)International version MY 593, fingerprint oplus/ossi/ossi:15/AP3A.240617.008/1755013304553
my_manifestChina 802: RMX6688_15.0.1.802(CN01), ota RMX6688_11.A.38_0380_202509082012

tee_bChina 802

vbmetaflags=3 (verification disabled, at offset 123 bytes)
  • A/B partitions plus Virtual A/B, current slot is b.
  • The international version has no 802 base package, so the port package uses the China package for the lower layer.
  • Do not use system OTA updates: my_manifest is China 802, so a China OTA might be pushed. This is an inference, not actually tested.

2. AOD Fix (completed, user has confirmed fixed)

  • Root cause: display_features.xml in the port package’s my_product came from International version 24749 (oha_support / fingeprint_optical_enabled). The fix was to replace it with the China 24618 configuration and remove disable_aod_all_day_mode.
  • Flashing: 2026-10-10, under fastbootd only my_product_b was flashed, image was my_product_B_allday.img (md5 3916e32a6e9e9cbb14165ae22b4f4894, 2557247488 B). This flash was approved by the user (“I agree that you can start flashing”), and the consent is valid only for this one time.
  • fastbootd driver: Requires Google USB driver (VID_18D1&PID_4EE0), r13 version, installed on this computer with pnputil /add-driver … /install.
  • Image location (the original F:\tmp\gt7aod\out has been deleted): O:\GT7_backup_20261010_copy\aod_fix\
    • my_product_B_allday.img: md5 3916e32a…, this is what is currently on the phone.
    • my_product_A_cn_exact.img: md5 39d437f5…, alternative plan A.
    • my_product_ORIGINAL_rollback.img: md5 6ef16441…, 2533498880 B, for rollback.
  • If the port package (flash.bat) is flashed again in the future, it will overwrite my_product back to the old version, and the B version image will need to be flashed again.

3. Backup

Partitions + mounted partitions (completed and verified)

  • C:\Users\Wray\GT7_backup_20261010\
    • partitions\: 103 physical partitions plus super.img, all compared with sha256 on the phone. In partitions\SHA256SUMS, nvdata appears on two lines; the last line ffd951a8… is authoritative.
    • Also logical\, mounted\, super_chunks\, _incomplete\.
    • data_ps1\: tar archives of mounted partitions have been verified; internal storage was only partially backed up, because the adb service disconnected midway and Android.tar was truncated.
    • data_full\: left over from an interrupted test on 2026-10-11, about 392MB, incomplete, can be deleted.
    • data\: empty directory.
  • Copy on the second disk: O:\GT7_backup_20261010_copy\, 124 files verified, also contains aod_fix\ and SHA256SUMS_copy.txt.
  • O:\DNA3-36-win\GT7_backup_20261010\: only text lists and a few directories, an early artifact.
  • User data (internal storage about 33GB, app data 65GB or more): the user said it had already been backed up before, so no full backup was made this time.

7z archives (in O:\DNA3-36-win\)

FileDescription
Realme GT7 For_EX01.7zOriginal port package, untouched
Realme GT7 For_EX01_本机一致版.7z7742841918 B, tested with 7zr t and CRC compared. Consistent with the phone’s current state: my_product is the fixed version, flash.bat has added my_company_a / my_manifest_a, tee is 802, init_boot is KernelSU, with init_boot_stock_A01.img and 修改说明.txt also attached. The positions recorded with lpdump were used to slice out each logical partition from super for comparison; the flash targets match slot b (except for vbmeta’s flag).
GT7_本机专属分区_3B1F5TE6K0YF1PRM_20261010.7z118514412 B, verified. Contains 22 device-specific partition images: nvdata, nvcfg, nvram, protect1/2, md_sec, persist, proinfo, seccfg, sec1, otp, oplusreserve1/2/3/5/6, metadata, para, boot_para, dram_para, expdb, frp; also tar archives of 5 mounted partitions, 说明.txt, SHA256SUMS.txt, getprop, by-name.   • tee is not different for every machine: the tee image is vendor-signed generic firmware. Each machine’s own keys and data are in partitions such as nvdata, protect, and md_sec (included in the device-specific package above).

4. General-purpose backup scripts

O:\DNA3-36-win\Android_full_backup.ps1 (PowerShell 5.1 / 7, UTF-8 BOM, CRLF)

  • Backup content:
    • When rooted: dd physical partitions (excluding userdata, swap, whole-disk devices, and duplicate devices); logical partitions are exported separately only when -AllLogical or -Only is added; writable mounted partitions are tarred; internal storage; app data under /data (split by app).
    • When not rooted: only backs up /sdcard and third-party app apks.
  • Verification method:
    • Partitions are compared with sha256 against the phone side; when a partition is being written by the system, the result of two consecutive identical reads is used.
    • Large partitions are read in chunks and can resume after interruption.
    • tar archives are compared by file count and byte count; hard links are counted only once by inode.
    • A tar archive must end with two all-zero blocks; otherwise it is considered incomplete.
  • Read-only guarantee: All commands sent to the phone go through a read-only check. Commands are first base64-encoded, then passed through adb exec-out "echo <b64>|base64 -d|su".
  • Issues fixed on 2026-10-11 according to review comments:
    • The read-only check mismatched quotes when encountering '\'' escapes.
    • On adb transfer errors, it now checks the exit code and stderr and retries; after consecutive failures it stops, and rerunning can resume.
    • In -Live mode, if the phone has files but the archive has none, it is no longer accepted.
    • When file names differ only by case, a hash is uniformly added to distinguish them (Clash).
    • Hard link deduplication.
    • Internal storage is all handled as -Live.
    • SHA256SUMS and logs changed to no BOM.
    • Free space check under network paths (UNC).
    • Wait-Device displays adb’s actual state.
    • In the non-root path, the package name of pm path has escaping added.
  • Real-device tests (read-only, -Only misc,frp,persist,nvdata,metadata) all passed.

O:\DNA3-36-win\android_full_backup.py (Python 3.8+, standard library only, cross-platform, LF, no BOM)

  • Functionally equivalent to the ps1. Output directory, file names, .ok markers, and SHA256SUMS are completely identical, and the two scripts can resume each other’s backups.
  • tar verification now uses Python’s tarfile; the RHT.security.selinux pax records generated by toybox can be parsed normally.
  • Porting process: 1 agent implemented, 3 reviewed by direction, 1 fixed, 1 offline tested, all using the default model. The review raised 11 issues, 9 were fixed. The two not changed: one is the tie order in partition sorting, which does not affect the result; the other is the way Clash is determined — actual testing showed that PowerShell hashtables are inherently case-insensitive, and the current implementation behaves the same as the ps1.
  • Offline tests were run with a fake adb and all passed: full backup, rerun skip, --only, non-root, transfer failure retry, truncated tar rejected, partition content changing during read, various special file names, hard links, read-only check.
  • Real-device tests (read-only, same set of partitions) passed. The hashes of misc, frp, and metadata are the same as in the ps1 run; nvdata and persist are written during runtime, so differing between the two runs is normal.
  • Incident record: The implementing agent once ran the script without adding the --adb parameter and connected to the real phone. Only read-only commands were executed (get-state, getprop, cat /proc/mounts, cat /proc/partitions, lpdump); there was no dd and no writing of any kind; the temporary text generated was deleted. The user was truthfully informed.
  • Note: The previously used Python virtual environment F:\tmp\gt7aod\venv was deleted along with tmp; from now on it needs to be run with the system Python.

5. Pitfalls encountered

  • adb stderr under PS 5.1: At ErrorActionPreference=Stop, it is treated as NativeCommandError, and needs to be changed locally to Continue.
  • Multiline here-string in CRLF scripts: \r must be removed before sending to the phone.
  • Checking with bsdtar after packing with toybox: The pax record written by tar --selinux has a trailing NUL, and bsdtar reports “malformed pax attributes”, but the content is intact. To determine whether an archive is complete, look at the two all-zero blocks at the end.
  • The adb service disconnecting midway truncates the tar: This is why transfer checks were added.
  • fastbootd cannot detect the phone: The Google USB driver needs to be installed.
  • Flashing a larger image: Logical partitions automatically expand.
  • Workflow scripts must not contain CR: Write with LF; a single agent’s output must be length-limited, otherwise it will exceed the 32k output limit.
  • Claude Pro quota: No more than 3 top-tier models running in parallel at the same time.

6. To-do / Optional

  • Delete C:\Users\Wray\GT7_backup_20261010\data_full (leftover from the interrupted test), pending the user’s decision.
  • If a complete user data backup is needed in the future, use either script with --no-partitions / -NoPartitions, and confirm the phone is unlocked before backing up.

Windows Mapped Drives to Achieve Linux-like Management

Registry subst+link

Ultimate Implementation Plan: Perform Global Mapping via the SYSTEM Account

Registry Execution

Windows’ kernel (Session Manager), at boot time, does read a specific registry path as SYSTEM to load drives. This is the DOS Devices we mentioned earlier.

  • The /v value must include a colon: it must be D:, not D.

  • The /d data must include the kernel escape prefix: it must be \??\C:\your_folder. Here, \??\ tells the Windows Object Manager that this is a direct local file system parse request.

After modification, remember to configure ACLs to avoid occasional permission issues.

icacls "C:\Tools" /grant:r "$($env:USERNAME):(OI)(CI)F" /T /C

Manual

We need to use “Task Scheduler” to have the system, at startup or user logon, use the identity of SYSTEM to silently execute subst.

Steps:

  1. Clean up remnants: First, execute subst D: /D in all terminals, and delete the previously tested registry mappings and SMB mappings to ensure the D drive is completely freed.
  2. Open Task Scheduler: Press Win + R, type taskschd.msc, and press Enter.
  3. Create the core task: In the right-hand Actions pane, click “Create Task…” (note: not “Create Basic Task”).
  4. Configure the [General] tab:
    • Name: enter any name, for example Global_Subst_D
    • Security options: click “Change User or Group” -> enter SYSTEM -> click “Check Names” (it will become NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) -> OK.
    • Check “Run with highest privileges” at the bottom.
  5. Configure the [Triggers] tab:
    • Click “New…”.
    • Begin the task: select “At log on”.
    • Settings: select “Any user”.
    • Click OK.
  6. Configure the [Actions] tab (key):
    • Click “New…”.
    • Action: select “Start a program”.
    • Program/script: enter cmd.exe
    • Add arguments: enter /c subst D: C:\cuda (replace C:\cuda with your actual deep directory path)
    • Click OK.
  7. Configure the [Conditions] tab:
    • Uncheck “Start the task only if the computer is on AC power” (to prevent it from failing when a laptop is on battery).
  8. Save and apply immediately:
    • Click “OK” to save the task.
    • In the task list, find the Global_Subst_D you just created, right-click it, and select “Run”.

Interface Traffic Splitting

MWAN3

Disable all hardware acceleration, firewall & wed

Because of public network traversal, for IPv6 it is best not to use load balancing when not using NAT6

  1. Register Interfaces: Register all interfaces you want to split traffic across

  2. Add Members: Create MWAN interfaces, set metric (priority), weight (traffic ratio)

  3. Set Policies: Bundle the required members (that need to be split together) into one policy. For public network allocation, a separate policy needs to be set here

  4. Set Rules: Destination address 0.0.0.0/0, i.e., split all external network IPs. For public network allocation, source address filtering needs to be set here.

Rules ultimately determine the effect. If you need to test, create a policy bound to a single interface and create a rule moved to the top
